text: Given an unsorted array nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers. It must run in linear time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Consecutive means values differing by one, and they need not be adjacent in the array — so one hundred, four, two hundred, one, three, two has the run one, two, three, four, length four? And duplicates just collapse — one, two, two, three is still length three?
Exactly. And note the hard linear-time requirement.
That linear-time constraint is the whole game — it rules out the obvious sort-then-scan, which is n log n. And an empty array should return zero.

Let me think about how to get linear time. This problem reminds me of hash-set membership — put everything in a hash set, and every lookup is constant time. A naive idea is, for each number, walk right counting x plus one, x plus two, and so on. That's quadratic on one through n, because every number re-walks the whole run. The fix: only start counting from a run's left end — a number x where x minus one is not in the set. Then each run is walked exactly once.

Here's the plan. One: put all the numbers in a set called seen. Two: for each value in the set, skip it if its left neighbor is also in the set. Three: otherwise walk right while the next value exists, and keep the longest length. One thing worth flagging — the key line is the skip. Without it, the answer is still correct, but it degrades to quadratic. With it, the amortized cost is linear: each number is examined once by the outer loop, and walked once by its run's start, so the inner while steps total n. One more thing — I iterate the set, not the array, so duplicates don't cause repeated examinations. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. I build the set straight from the array, which dedupes it. Then for each value, if s minus one is in the set, I continue; otherwise I count right from s and update the max. One thing worth flagging — s is a by-value copy in the range-for, so incrementing it inside the while doesn't disturb the outer iteration over the set.

Let's dry-run one hundred, four, two hundred, one, three, two — expected four. The set iterates in no particular order, but that doesn't matter. The row that matters is one: zero isn't in the set, so one is a left end, and it walks one, two, three, four — length four. The interior members two, three, and four all get skipped, so the run is walked only once. Answer four. That matches. Corner cases: an empty array gives zero, since the loop never runs. One, two, two, three gives three, because the duplicate collapses in the set. A single element gives one. All check out.

Time is linear, amortized — each number is examined once and walked at most once, so despite the nested loop, the total is linear. Space is linear for the set. One more thing — the linear time relies on average-case constant-time hashing. If I needed a guaranteed worst case or no extra set, I'd trade down to the n log n sort — it avoids both the hash-collision risk and the extra memory.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: you saw that the linear-time constraint kills sorting, you nailed why the left-end guard turns a quadratic-looking loop into linear, and you iterated the set to keep the amortization clean. Good work.
